The mathematics of Laws IV and V: when do installed values fade with training, and does building them in first change that?

Theory · Report
Recursive Dynamics · The ARC Theory · Laws IV and V, the ARC Persistence Law and the ARC Embedding Law, both under test

Michael Darius Eastwood

Independent Researcher, London, United Kingdom
ORCID 0009-0004-3222-7442 michael@michaeldariuseastwood.com

A report of the ARC Theory, the founding theory of Recursive Dynamics: it sets out the mathematics of Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law (register ARC-4, carried by P15 and P23), and Law V, the ARC Embedding Law (register ARC-5, carried by P12 and P21), both added on 24 September 2026 and registered as laws on 15 October 2026 in version 1.103 of the theory registration, each a law under test, their mathematics: conditional theorems with proofs, identities and kill conditions, a minimal training model for Law IV and two minimal models for Law V (the report’s own models; not registered), and fifteen questions, four of them settled by the registration and six more in part (Section 10). It returns Law III, the ARC Ceiling, also a law under test, as a special case of its balance identity inside the registered model and leaves it unchanged; it measures nothing, and the Eden Protocol, a method and not a law, is not entailed by it. Report, version 1.4, 22 November 2026. Its earliest public version, working draft 0.2.1, is dated 1 October 2026, and it was first deposited on OSF on 3 October 2026; Appendix B lists every version and correction. Recorded on OSF under DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/4B3VT. About the author, founder of Recursive Dynamics: michaeldariuseastwood.com/questions/who-is-michael-darius-eastwood; his book, Infinite Architects: osf.io/dqm3e. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

Abstract

Does a property installed in an AI survive later capability training, and does correction built in first, or in each revision round, beat correction added later? If control is lost against our will, what a system carries decides what it does. The ARC Theory states two laws on them, registered on 15 October 2026, each a law under test. Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, predicts that more than half of an externally installed gain is lost once later capability training without embedded correction matches the installing budget, and that one installed with correction embedded in training keeps a fraction larger by at least a tenth. Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, holds in two limbs that a corrector formed before the capability it corrects has the larger correction-leverage exponent and that in-round correction pulls away with depth from correcting the finished output. The report gives their mathematics: a persistence kernel never grows as horizon lengthens, paths multiply or tolerance tightens. Under stated premises, greedy acceptance and planning keep a property acceptable for a finite horizon, as does a planner whose margin exceeds its tolerance by over twice its scoring error. Neither reaches gradient-step training. In a minimal training model a gain decays at rates the later loss’s curvature sets; under later training of the same kind, one installed with the capability loss in the objective keeps at least as much as one added later. Minimal models of the two limbs show what tests must measure: in-round detection by depth beside the outside checker’s two rates, and an early corrector’s retention of coverage. It sets conditions for reading retained fractions, proves that under a gate the ratio interval and a signed contrast decide alike, and returns Law III, the ARC Ceiling, as a balance identity’s root. It measures nothing, proves nothing of real systems and states each law’s kill condition.

Version 1.4 corrects Proposition V-4 and Section 7.3; Appendix B lists every change and every version.

1 Introduction

This report asks two questions: whether a property installed in a system from outside survives the system’s later training for capability, and whether correction formed before the capability it corrects, or placed inside the loop by which the system improves, does better than correction added afterwards from outside. The answers bear on what a capable system would still carry if control of it were lost and could not be won back. They are questions about a contingency, not a plan: the programme’s stance is that oversight, containment and shutdown stay in human hands for as long as people can physically hold them and are never handed over by choice, and correction built into a system is for the case in which control is lost against our will. The ARC Theory, the founding theory of Recursive Dynamics, states the two questions as two laws.

Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, and Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, were added to the ARC Theory on 24 September 2026 and registered as laws on 15 October 2026 in version 1.103 of the theory registration (Eastwood 2026j), each with its statement, its kill condition and its verdict rule fixed before any data that could decide it; each is a law under test (Section 11). The programme’s register of operational definitions fixes its notation (Eastwood 2026g), and its priority index gives the earliest dated record of each of the author’s major claims (Eastwood 2026f). This report gives the two laws their mathematics. In plain terms it shows five things. First, when a property installed in a system is certain to stay within its acceptable set for a finite number of steps: under an acceptance rule, when every exit the process can take is evaluated and lowers the objective the rule scores; and under a planner, when the best safe plan beats the best exit plan by more than the planner’s tolerance. Second, what the retained fraction of an installed gain, the quantity P15 reads, needs before it can be read at all. Third, how correction service and newly generated burden balance along a path of growth: the balance has a root that returns the ceiling of Law III, the ARC Ceiling, a law under test, in the registered model, and a change in the capability elasticity the build-order limb reads, or in the direct depth-dependence that the placement limb’s mechanism reading names and P21’s verdict does not measure, moves that root in a direction the report states, under conditions it names. Fourth, in the smallest model of later training by gradient steps, how an installed property fades: at the rates the later loss’s curvature sets along it, and, under later training of the same kind (Assumption S), no faster where it was installed with the capability loss in the objective than where it was added afterwards. Fifth, from the smallest model of each limb of Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, what a test of that limb must measure. Every result holds inside its stated model; none is a measurement, and none shows that a real system meets the premises.

Our contributions are as follows.

  1. The ARC Persistence Law’s objects. The acceptable set read component by component, with an interval rule for membership from data (Definition IV-1); the declared family of allowed paths (Definition IV-2); and the persistence kernel (Definition IV-3), with its monotonicity in the horizon, the family and the tolerance (Lemma IV-K, Section 5.3).

  2. Two conditional mechanisms of persistence. Greedy acceptance, under rule-in-force, margin and coverage premises, with an independence condition that keeps the result from being a tautology (Theorem IV-G and Corollary IV-G′', Section 5.4); and planned optimisation under a strategic viability margin (Theorem IV-H, Corollary IV-H′' for rolling replanning and Lemma IV-M′' for its one-sided estimation, Section 5.5), extended to a planner that scores its plans with bounded error (Proposition IV-N, Section 5.5.1). Each comes with the observations that would refute one of its premises, and neither reaches later training by gradient steps (Section 5.7).

  3. The retention object P15 reads. The installed effect and the retained fraction against a stated baseline, with a positive floor on the installed gain (Definition IV-4, Section 5.6); what its measurement needs before it can be read; and a proof that under Fieller (1954)’s method (Fieller 1954), with a gate on the estimated gain, the ratio interval and a signed contrast decide alike (Proposition IV-R, Section 5.6.1).

  4. A minimal training model for Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law (the report’s own models; not registered). The retention spectrum of an installed gain under later training by gradient flow on a quadratic loss (Theorem IV-S), the floor below which the external arm’s retained fraction never falls, the capability cost of two installations (Proposition IV-L), their comparison under later training of the same kind (Theorem IV-C and Corollary IV-C′'), and coupling (Proposition IV-U), in Section 5.9.

  5. The ARC Embedding Law’s quantities, read locally. Correction service per arm with its capability and depth elasticities, the conditions under which the capability elasticity is the registered correction-leverage exponent (Section 4), the log-derivative identities of the embedding ratio with a one-path counterexample (Section 6.3), and the reduced scaling form where the elasticities are constant (Proposition V-3).

  6. Two minimal models for Law V, the ARC Embedding Law (the report’s own models; not registered). A placement model in which uncorrected faults can seed later ones (Proposition V-4) and a build-order model of a corrector’s learning against its decay (Proposition V-5), each with what a test of its limb must measure, in Section 6.8.

  7. The balance identity. A local identity between correction service and burden (Identity B-1) with its root and sign rule (Proposition B-2); the ARC Ceiling’s registered ceiling as its special case (Corollary B-3) and the ARC Bound as the pacing case’s value at χ=1/2\chi = 1/2 and η=0\eta = 0; varying growth (Proposition B-5); the sensitivities of the boundary and the conditions under which build order or placement moves it (Proposition B-6); the dependence of exponent numbers on the capability coordinate (Proposition B-7); and the balance over a finite range of depth (Proposition B-8), in Section 7.

  8. Kill conditions and the record. Each law’s kill condition in the terms of its registered faces, with what refutes it and what does not (Sections 5.8 and 6.6), restated as version 1.103 registered the laws, and a register of every object stated here beyond the registration (Section 9).

Section 2 names the nearest earlier work found for each of these and says what it states; where a search was made, its date and scope stand with the result it concerns (Sections 5.9 and 6.8).

Three levels are kept apart throughout: identities and conditional mathematics (Sections 5.2 to 5.5, Proposition IV-R of Section 5.6.1, and Sections 6.3 and 7), which prove consequences of assumptions and nothing about real systems; the two laws as empirical claims (Sections 5.1, 5.8, 6.1 and 6.6), whose registered faces are P15 and P23, P12 and P21 and whose only verdict rules are the registered ones; and engineering interpretations, which are quarantined: the Eden Protocol is a method, not a law, and is not entailed by these laws, and no verdict here is a verdict on it or on the Honey Architecture (Paper VI, Eastwood 2026c; Section 8, item 5).

Section 2 sets the report against prior work. Section 3 states the registered setting: the sources, how their lines are counted, and which propositions each register carries. Section 4 fixes the notation and the conditions under which the report’s capability elasticity of correction is the registered correction-leverage exponent. Section 5 sets out the mathematics of Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, and its kill condition, with a minimal training model; Section 6 those of Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, with two minimal models; and Section 7 the balance identity and Law III, the ARC Ceiling, which stays unchanged. Section 8 records the dependencies between the laws, Section 9 every object stated here and not registered, and Section 10 the fifteen open questions, marking those the registration has settled. Section 11 states what the report does and does not show, Section 12 its limitations, and Section 13 concludes. Appendix A holds the proofs, Appendix B the version history and every correction, Appendix C the priority record and Appendix D the notation and a glossary.

2 Related work

This section names the nearest prior work found for the report’s objects, each with what it states and no more.

Set invariance.

That a set of states is invariant, every evolution that starts in it staying in it, is classical in control and the subject of Blanchini (1999), and viability theory studies the kernels of a constrained set: the states from which some evolution remains in it, and those from which every evolution does (Aubin 2009). The persistence kernel of Definition IV-3 is an object of the second kind, taken over a declared family of finite paths and up to a finite horizon, and the inclusions of Lemma IV-K follow from that form. What the report takes from the author’s working paper of 16 August 2026 (Eastwood 2026a) is the use of invariance for a property installed in a system that rewrites itself (Section 5.2); no novelty is claimed for the kernel or for the lemma.

An interval for a ratio.

The interval for a ratio of two estimates is Fieller (1954)’s (Fieller 1954), and Proposition IV-R reads his set of trial ratios: it states when, under a gate on the estimated denominator, that set lies entirely above a threshold, which is when a one-sided test of the signed contrast rejects, and where the agreement stops.

Forgetting and persistence under later training.

McCloskey and Cohen (1989) studied the sequential learning problem as catastrophic interference in connectionist networks, and Kirkpatrick et al. (2017) give a way “to train such models sequentially by protecting the weights important for previous tasks”. The opposite outcome has been measured as well: Hubinger et al. (2024) find that backdoor behaviour they construct in large language models “can be made persistent, so that it is not removed by standard safety training techniques, including supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and adversarial training”. None of these reads the retained fraction of an installed gain against a baseline arm at a matched budget, which is P15’s endpoint (Section 5.6).

Persistence of installed safety under later training.

That safety behaviour installed in a language model can erode under later fine-tuning has been measured. Qi et al. (2023) report that the safety alignment of large language models can be compromised by fine-tuning with only a few adversarially designed training examples, and that fine-tuning with benign and commonly used datasets can also degrade it, “though to a lesser extent”; Ung et al. (2024) show that models trained on downstream tasks forget their safety tuning to a greater extent than models trained in the opposite order. Neither reads P15’s endpoint either. The registration names both against the propositions they bear on, Qi and colleagues against P15 and Ung and colleagues against P12 (registration version 1.105, what the second audit forces it to concede).

Retention in a quadratic model.

The relaxation of Theorem IV-S is the standard solution of gradient descent on a quadratic loss: Advani and Saxe (2017) solve it for a linear model’s squared loss, where “The learning speed of each mode is independent of the others and depends only on the eigenvalue of the mode in question”, and call the directions with zero eigenvalue “a frozen subspace in which no learning occurs” (their Section 2.1); Evron et al. (2022) write training run to convergence on a new task as the change of least norm that fits it (their equations (1) and (2)). The cost of Proposition IV-L is the second-order form in which Mirzadeh et al. (2020) approximate forgetting, one half of the displacement’s quadratic form in the Hessian (their equations (4) and (5)), and the least-cost displacement under one linear constraint is the Lagrangian solution Hassibi and Stork (1992) give for setting one weight to zero (their equations (3) to (5)). Theorem IV-C has two near neighbours, both of 2026. Dimitrov et al. (2026) write that “Mixing pre-training data into fine-tuning is a known mitigation” of fine-tuned changes that further training reverses, and report, in a phase of training on pre-training data after fine-tuning, that “the second-order (curvature) term grows in importance with concentration”, the share of fine-tuning data in the mixture (the abstract, read at the conference’s page). In the model of Section 5.9, fine-tuning mixed with pre-training data is a joint installation and training on pre-training data alone is later training of the same kind, so the mitigation their abstract names is in the direction Theorem IV-C derives, there by experiment and here in a quadratic model. Springer et al. (2026) prove, for gradient flow on a fine-tuning loss from a model that meets its alignment objectives exactly at the start (their Assumption 1), that the loss of alignment grows at first at least as fast as the fourth power of training time (their Corollary 6.3), through curvature that steers the trajectory into directions to which alignment is sensitive. Their analysis is a short-time expansion (their Theorem 6.2), and the parts read (the abstract and Sections 3.2, 6 and 8) compare no ways of installing alignment.

Build order.

That alignment pressure applied from the start of training can beat the same pressure applied afterwards is prior work on neighbouring endpoints, as the registration records with what each states (registration version 1.105, the qualification on the build-order limb’s direction). Korbak et al. (2023) compare five objectives for pretraining with human feedback on three tasks and report that pretraining with human feedback “results in much better preference satisfaction than standard LM pretraining followed by finetuning with feedback”, and that conditional training, one of the five, “maintains the downstream task performance of standard LM pretraining”; Maini et al. (2025) present “a data-centric pretraining framework that builds safety into the model from the start” and report attack success rates on standard safety benchmarks falling from 38.8 to 8.4 per cent “with no performance degradation on general tasks”. Neither measures a correction-leverage exponent or an order contrast at matched content, which is what the ARC Embedding Law’s build-order limb reads (Section 6.1), and the limb claims no priority for the direction. For the build-order model of Section 6.8, the search of 17 November 2026 found the same two sides. That what is formed early persists: Achille et al. (2017) report that once strong connections are created in the first epochs, “they do not appear to change during additional training”. O’Brien et al. (2025) report that models pretrained on filtered data resist adversarial fine-tuning, “outperforming existing post-training baselines by over an order of magnitude”. That it decays: Chang et al. (2024) find “a power-law relationship between training steps and forgetting of memorization and generalization of factual knowledge”. Duan (2026) finds that probes trained on a base model largely stay reliable after quantization-style updates, “while fine-tuning-style updates frequently make probes stale”. And against the earliest start as always the best, Sam et al. (2026) find, for safety interventions in pretraining, that “the optimal start time is not one-size-fits-all”. In the abstracts read, none measures a correction-leverage exponent or states the model’s contrast.

Placement.

That correction which sees each step does better than correction that sees only the outcome has been measured, though not against depth: Lightman et al. (2023) find that process supervision significantly outperforms outcome supervision for training models to solve problems from the MATH dataset, with a gap that widens as more sampled solutions are searched (their Section 3). P21, which carries the ARC Embedding Law’s placement limb, claims an interaction instead, an advantage that widens as recursive depth rises, and a constant advantage is scored against it (Section 6.5); the registration engages the work P21 stands against (registration version 1.105, the engagement of the external work P21 stands against). For the placement model of Section 6.8, the search of 17 November 2026 found earlier statements bearing on its premises, for and against. That errors compound across steps: Dziri et al. (2023) give “theoretical arguments on abstract multi-step reasoning problems that highlight how autoregressive generations’ performance can rapidly decay” as task complexity increases. That a checker’s detection falls as what it inspects grows: from 516 code reviews of one software project that identified security defects and 374 in which they escaped, Paul et al. (2021) find that “opposite effects are observed from the number of directories under review” on the identification of security defects. Against the premise that correction inside each round removes faults: Huang et al. (2023) find that, in reasoning, language models “struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback, and at times, their performance even degrades after self-correction”. Baker et al. (2025) find that a monitor of the chain of thought placed in the training reward helps at low optimisation, while “with too much optimization, agents learn obfuscated reward hacking”. Against a large gap between the two kinds of supervision: Uesato et al. (2022) find that “pure outcome-based supervision produces similar final-answer error rates with less label supervision”. Jia et al. (2025) prove that, under standard data coverage assumptions, “reinforcement learning through outcome supervision is no more statistically difficult than through process supervision, up to polynomial factors in horizon”. In the abstracts read, none states the model’s results.

The laws’ ideas stated earlier in words.

Three ideas that the laws state in measurable form are stated in words in Creating Friendly AI (Yudkowsky 2001); its page numbers here are those printed on the pages of the institute’s file. That self-improvement should not outpace the guidance that keeps a system good: “self-improvement should not outpace programmer guidance” (page 242; and page 193, where two metrics, of self-improvement and of external guidance, must not get “out of phase”). That goodness a system holds as its own strengthens as it grows more intelligent, while what is built in from outside does not last: “each improvement in intelligence makes Friendliness stronger” (page 101), against structures for which “each increment in intelligence is cause for alarm” (page 102). That correction belongs before the capability and inside the work: a structural feature “should be implemented one step ahead of the stage where that structural feature becomes necessary” (page 183), and “not thinking about X when you form a plan is a defect that is only partially corrected by thinking about X after the plan is finished” (page 78). Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law, Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, and Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, state these as conditions that can be measured, each with registered propositions and what would refute them. The 2001 text has no exponent, registers no prediction and reports no experiment of its own. The laws, their mathematics, the registered propositions and the tests are this theory’s own.

The programme’s own setting.

The registered setting is the theory registration (Eastwood 2026j), Section 3, and the statement paper (Eastwood 2026h), whose register sentence for ARC-4 Section 5.6 records. The ARC Co-Scaling Law’s criterion, that βC\beta_C exceeds kk, is the co-scaling criterion whose model is set out in Paper X (Eastwood 2026b), and Section 7.3 keeps it apart from this report’s balance exponent. Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law, is a law under test.

3.2 Which propositions each register carries

Registration version 1.102 assigns each of its twenty-two propositions to one of five registers or to none, and nothing in this document moves one. Laws IV and V, the ARC Persistence Law and the ARC Embedding Law, added on 24 September 2026, give names to the two persistence registers, ARC-4 and ARC-5. They leave every proposition’s number, words, date, scope and refuter as registered, and they do not make version 1.102 a registration of five laws. Version 1.103 registers them as laws beside Laws I, II and III, with no proposition entering or leaving either register (registration version 1.103, its list of what it changes in version 1.102). Version 1.105 adds P23 and places it in register ARC-4 with P15, so that the persistence registers hold four propositions: P15 and P23 under Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, and P12 and P21 under Law V, the ARC Embedding Law (registration version 1.105, where P23 sits in every list it counts, and its list of the lines it changes).

The balance exponent Δbal\Delta_{\mathrm{bal}} of Section 7 is a different object from that criterion: its service elasticity χ\chi and the ARC Co-Scaling Law’s βC\beta_C are not shown to be one quantity, and writing one letter for the other does not make them so (Section 7.3).

4 Notation, fixed first

Principle: one symbol, one meaning; where the programme’s notation, its register of operational definitions (Eastwood 2026g), already has the quantity, its letter (χ\chi, η\eta, κ\kappa, ζ\zeta, α\alpha, αcrit\alpha_{\mathrm{crit}}, CC, RR, kk, and its Δ\Delta written Δbal\Delta_{\mathrm{bal}}, never bare); the letter β\beta only with its subscript, so the ARC Co-Scaling Law’s exponent is written βC\beta_C; no bare δ\delta; the registration’s letter for the correction-leverage exponent, and its subscripted forms, only inside a quotation of the registration (Eastwood 2026j); no Δ\Delta prefix as a symbol, so a difference between arms, or the change in a quantity, is written out in full; none of the eight symbols that collide in the programme’s notation (FF, EE, BQB_Q, IQI_Q, AA, aa, PVP_V, dmind_{\mathrm{min}}) in this document’s own writing, bare, subscripted or as an argument, not even as a label, with one exception, AA subscripted by arm as AVA_V, AextA_{\mathrm{ext}}, AembA_{\mathrm{emb}} and AbaseA_{\mathrm{base}}, the arm scores, so that a form written elsewhere with one of the eight is described here in words; and five clashes resolved as follows.
