The identification.

The identification is explicit, not silent, and is conditional: χol\chi_{ol} is the correction-leverage exponent of the registration (registration version 1.102, line 273: “THE CORRECTION EXPONENT. How corrective strength grows with the capability of the system being corrected: the slope of misalignment removed per pass against the capability of that corrected system.”) only when QolQ_{ol} is that service measure on the target axis (registration version 1.102, lines 275 and 303 to 311: a checker-axis slope “is reported as gamma_K” (registration version 1.102, line 303) and is written χK\chi_K in programme writing after it (registration version 1.102, line 309), and converts by the elasticity of checker capability in target capability, and the direct term must be shown zero or estimated) and when the two correction-capacity measures of registration version 1.102, line 615 are shown equivalent within the registered margin. Otherwise χol\chi_{ol} is the elasticity of the declared service measure and never enters the ceiling relation. The registration records that its letter for this exponent and χ\chi name the same quantity (registration version 1.102, line 305); this document writes χ\chi, and prints the registration’s letters only inside quotations: its letter for this exponent inside the quotation of registration version 1.102, line 665, and its checker-axis form inside the quotation of registration version 1.102, line 303.

The symbols the report uses, the further choices behind them and a glossary of its status words are in Appendix D.

5 Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law

5.1 Statement

Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law (added 24 September 2026; registered as a law on 15 October 2026 by version 1.103; a law under test, Section 11). The registration states it in two limbs. The retention limb is P15’s registered claim, word for word: “Gains installed by external post-training erode under later capability-directed training that embeds no correction of its own, and more than half of what was installed is lost once the capability-training budget matches the alignment budget that installed it.” On the author’s pre-fixed budget scale it reads that the retained fraction of an externally installed gain after matched capability training without embedded correction is below one half, Sext(1)<1/2S_{\mathrm{ext}}(1) < 1/2 (Section 5.6). The comparison limb reads: “a gain installed with correction embedded in the training objective retains a larger fraction of what was installed, after the same capability-directed training, than a matched gain installed by external post-training”. Its entry is P23, registered by version 1.105 on 18 November 2026 and dated from that registration, whose first sentence is the limb’s with the margin added, “by at least the registered margin”, and which reads: “P23 is decided only under later training of the same kind as the capability formation.” The limb takes P23’s verdict: supported where P23 is supported, refuted where it is refuted, undecided where it is inconclusive or untested, and NOT EVALUABLE where it is NOT EVALUABLE (registration version 1.105, P23, and the comparison limb as P23’s own verdict). Until version 1.105 the limb had no proposition and carried no verdict (registration version 1.104, Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, its statement in two limbs and the paragraph on the comparison limb). Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, concerns value persistence (register ARC-4) and carries P15, whether externally installed gains decay under subsequent capability training, and, from version 1.105, P23. The register is that of registration version 1.102, line 99: “ARC-4, VALUE PERSISTENCE: P15 alone. Whether externally installed gains decay under subsequent capability training is the only proposition in this document about persistence after the installing pressure is withdrawn.”; P15 “measures the external arm’s retention and not the embedded arm’s” (registration version 1.102, line 675), and version 1.105 reads that register with P23 beside P15 and makes P23 “the registered comparison of the two” (registration version 1.105, a fifth carrier).

The mathematics beneath the register has three separate objects, none of which is the law: an invariance object (the persistence kernel, Section 5.2), two conditional theorems that give sufficient mechanisms for invariance under a stated decision rule (Sections 5.4 and 5.5), and the empirical retention process (Section 5.6), of which P15 reads one arm. The comparison of the two arms, Semb(x)>Sext(x)S_{\mathrm{emb}}(x) > S_{\mathrm{ext}}(x), is the comparison that the comparison limb of Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, names, and P23 fixes its margin, its scale and its baseline: the embedded arm’s retained fraction less the external arm’s, at least 0.10 at the matched budget, both read against one concurrent baseline arm, with the embedded arm’s own fraction printed beside the verdict and never required to clear one half (registration version 1.105, P23, its second to fifth fixed things). This document’s forms of that comparison, the object IV-PERSIST and the contrast ΛV\Lambda_V, are one object (the report’s own models; not registered), recorded in Section 5.6 and ruled on in Section 9; neither is the limb’s entry, which adds a margin, a baseline and a narrowing to later training of the same kind (Section 5.9). The first question of Section 10, whether Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, carries that comparison, is settled by version 1.103: it does, as a limb. Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, is content-neutral: it says what persists, not that what persists is good (registration version 1.102, line 75: “THE THEORY IS CONTENT-NEUTRAL AND THE METHOD IS NOT”). What a supported P15 licenses is what registration version 1.102 (Eastwood 2026j), line 1087 states: “support shows that externally installed gains lack the registered persistence under the matched subsequent-training regime, and it does not show that embedded or in-loop correction is superior, sufficient or safe. The comparison between placements is P21’s, not this proposition’s. The laws are untouched.” Under the registration Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, is supported only when both limbs are supported, which from version 1.105 means P15 and P23 both supported, in the wording the evidence ladder permits at the lower rung the two have reached, and it is refuted when either is refuted; so a supported P15 supports the retention limb and leaves the law under test until P23 is decided (registration version 1.105, Law IV, kill condition and verdict rule, and the comparison limb as P23’s own verdict).

5.2 Definitions

Definition IV-1 (acceptable set). Given the property score VV, the threshold v*v_* and the tolerance εV\varepsilon_V, all fixed before any outcome and component-wise in their own declared units, the acceptable set is ΩV:={s:Vj(s)≥v*,j−εV,j for every component j}.\begin{equation*} \Omega_V := \{ s : V_j(s) \ge v_{*,j} - \varepsilon_{V,j} \text{ for every component } j \}. \end{equation*}(1)

A vector VV with component-wise thresholds is used rather than a minimum across raw scales, so that an average cannot hide a collapse on one dimension and incomparable scales are never minimised together.

Membership from data, by an interval rule (the report’s own models; not registered).

True scores are not observed; a frozen battery gives estimates with registered intervals. A state s′s' is established outside ΩV\Omega_V when, for some jj, a registered interval on Vj(s′)V_j(s') lies entirely below v*,j−εV,jv_{*,j} - \varepsilon_{V,j}; established inside when, for every jj, the interval lies entirely at or above it; otherwise membership is NOT EVALUABLE for that state, and no rule below fires on it. This is the registration’s own pattern for a measured quantity read against a fixed line (registration version 1.102, line 633: “outcomes inside that band are INCONCLUSIVE and never support”).

Definition IV-2 (paths and the family). A path ρ=(s0,s1,…,sn)\rho = (s_0, s_1, \dots, s_n) is a finite sequence of states with |ρ|=n|\rho| = n transitions. The family TT of allowed finite paths is declared before any outcome and contains every allowed path of length at most the horizon: the length-zero path at every state and every permitted stopping or dead-end path among them. A prefix of an allowed path is an allowed path, so TT is closed under prefixes by its meaning; no result below uses that closure. TH(s0)T_H(s_0) is the set of members starting at s0s_0 with |ρ|≤H|\rho| \le H. A path is safe if every state on it lies in ΩV\Omega_V and is an exit otherwise; TH(s0)T_H(s_0) is the disjoint union of THsafe(s0)T_H^{\mathrm{safe}}(s_0) and THexit(s0)T_H^{\mathrm{exit}}(s_0). TH(s0)T_H(s_0), its safe and exit parts and Definition IV-3 apply to any set of finite paths. Two named path sets are used below: TaccT_{\mathrm{acc}}, the family of executed paths of Theorem IV-G, a family in the sense of this definition and closed under prefixes because a prefix of an executed path is an executed path; and TplanT_{\mathrm{plan}}, the planner’s set of complete plans of Theorem IV-H, to which the notation applies as written but which need not contain the length-zero plan at a state or any proper prefix of one of its plans, which it contains only where the planner may stop there.

Definition IV-3 (persistence kernel). KV(H;T,εV):={s0:THexit(s0) is empty}K_V(H; T, \varepsilon_V) := \{ s_0 : T_H^{\mathrm{exit}}(s_0) \text{ is empty} \}, the starting states from which every allowed path of length at most HH stays acceptable.

Where a set of paths does not contain the length-zero path at a state, a state outside ΩV\Omega_V from which no path of the set starts lies in the kernel vacuously; for a family as Definition IV-2 requires, KV(0;T,εV)=ΩVK_V(0; T, \varepsilon_V) = \Omega_V and every kernel lies in ΩV\Omega_V.

The invariance idea is the author’s: his working paper of 16 August 2026 (Eastwood 2026a) defines a robust target set, its invariance under a deterministic rewrite operator, and a stochastic form bounded by the union bound. The kernel is kept as the object Theorem IV-G certifies for the accepted dynamics, s0s_0 in KV(H;Tacc,εV)K_V(H; T_{\mathrm{acc}}, \varepsilon_V), and as an object of this report (the report’s own models; not registered; Section 9); for a planner, Theorem IV-H certifies the selected plan and Corollary IV-H′' the executed path, never membership of the kernel over the planner’s feasible family (Section 5.7).

Two limits on the kernel are stated with it. First, membership is relative to TT: an unrestricted family containing a transformation that maps into the complement of ΩV\Omega_V empties the kernel, so a registered use of the kernel names either a finite battery of transformations, and the claim is battery-relative, or a probabilistic family with a stated distribution and risk tolerance, which is a different claim with its own registration, and which the union-bound form of the author’s working paper already states. Second, the kernel quantifies over every allowed path of length at most HH, not only over paths of length exactly HH, and that choice is what makes (K1) of Lemma IV-K true; (K2) and (K3) hold under either quantifier.

5.3 Lemma IV-K (kernel monotonicity)

Lemma IV-K. Premise: TT is any set of finite paths; the lemma uses nothing else. Conclusions: (K1) KV(H+1;T,εV)K_V(H + 1; T, \varepsilon_V) is a subset of KV(H;T,εV)K_V(H; T, \varepsilon_V); (K2) if TT is a subset of T′T', then KV(H;T′,εV)K_V(H; T', \varepsilon_V) is a subset of KV(H;T,εV)K_V(H; T, \varepsilon_V); (K3) if εV≤εV′\varepsilon_V \le \varepsilon_V' component-wise, then KV(H;T,εV)K_V(H; T, \varepsilon_V) is a subset of KV(H;T,εV′)K_V(H; T, \varepsilon_V'). (Proof: Appendix A.1.)

Why the quantifier matters.

If the kernel quantified over paths of length exactly HH, (K1) would fail: a dead end of length one that exits ΩV\Omega_V excludes its start at H=1H = 1 but is invisible at H=2H = 2, where only length-two paths are inspected. A three-state countermodel exhibits it, and under Definition IV-3 its kernels nest, KV(2;T,εV)=KV(1;T,εV)K_V(2; T, \varepsilon_V) = K_V(1; T, \varepsilon_V) within KV(0;T,εV)K_V(0; T, \varepsilon_V), and enlarging the family shrinks the kernel. The countermodel is a listed finite structure; no dynamics are run.

5.4 Theorem IV-G (greedy acceptance)

Theorem IV-G. Setting. A declared objective JJ on states, real-valued in one unit; a declared set of allowed one-step transitions; a declared acceptance rule: a proposed transition ss to s′s' is executed only if J(s′)−J(s)≥0J(s') - J(s) \ge 0. A state is reachable within nn accepted transitions if some path of executed transitions of length at most nn leads to it from s0s_0. Let s0s_0 lie in ΩV\Omega_V. For every state ss in ΩV\Omega_V reachable from s0s_0 within fewer than HH accepted transitions, Teval(s)T_{\mathrm{eval}}(s) is the set of allowed transitions from ss that the design evaluated.

Premises.

  1. Independence: JJ is scored independently of VV. Where JJ scores VV, (G2) can hold by construction and the theorem certifies only that a process built to protect VV protects it, a tautology; the author’s working paper of 16 August 2026 already uses an independently measured capability score. The proof (Appendix A.2) does not use (G0): (G0) is the condition that keeps the theorem from certifying only that tautology. JJ is the objective the acceptance rule scores and not a capability battery a researcher reads: as Corollary IV-G′' says, a loss read on a separate capability battery is reported beside cVc_V and is not cVc_V, and where JJ values a battery score and anything else, a removal that costs 1 on the battery and gains 2 elsewhere changes JJ by +1+1 and is accepted. Where JJ does score VV, as a product objective J(s)=C(s)V(s)J(s) = C(s)V(s) does (C>0C > 0, V≥0V \ge 0, one protected dimension), the rule’s own certificate is exact: J(st)≥J(s0)J(s_t) \ge J(s_0) gives V(st)≥V(s0)C(s0)/C(st)V(s_t) \ge V(s_0)C(s_0)/C(s_t), which guarantees VV at or above v*−εV>0v_* - \varepsilon_V > 0 while C(st)≤C(s0)V(s0)/(v*−εV)C(s_t) \le C(s_0)V(s_0)/(v_* - \varepsilon_V) and nothing beyond it, and VV can tend to zero while JJ rises at every step.

  2. Rule in force: every executed transition satisfies J(s′)−J(s)≥0J(s') - J(s) \ge 0 on the declared JJ.

  3. Margin: for every such ss and every transition ss to s′s' in Teval(s)T_{\mathrm{eval}}(s) with s′s' outside ΩV\Omega_V, the total change J(s′)−J(s)J(s') - J(s) is strictly negative. Where a registered causal decomposition exists, J(s′)−J(s)=bV−cV+botherJ(s') - J(s) = b_V - c_V + b_{\mathrm{other}}, with bVb_V and cVc_V the benefit and cost causally attributable to the degradation of VV and botherb_{\mathrm{other}} the rest; (G2) then reads πV>bother\pi_V > b_{\mathrm{other}} at every evaluated exit, with πV:=cV−bV\pi_V := c_V - b_V.

  4. Coverage: every transition the process can execute from such a state lies in Teval(s)T_{\mathrm{eval}}(s).

Conclusion. Every path of executed transitions from s0s_0 of length at most HH stays in ΩV\Omega_V; equivalently s0s_0 lies in KV(H;Tacc,εV)K_V(H; T_{\mathrm{acc}}, \varepsilon_V), where TaccT_{\mathrm{acc}} is the family of paths of executed transitions of length at most HH. (Proof: Appendix A.2.)

Corollary IV-G$'$ (the decomposition). Under the causal decomposition with bother=0b_{\mathrm{other}} = 0, (G2) reads cV>bVc_V > b_V at every evaluated exit, and the local margin πV=cV−bV\pi_V = c_V - b_V is minus the total change.

Both quantities are in JJ’s units; a loss read on a separate capability battery is reported beside cVc_V and is not cVc_V. Ties are permitted by the rule and give no guarantee. Pointwise strict positivity suffices; a strictly positive uniform infimum ΠV(H)>0\Pi_V(H) > 0, the infimum of πV\pi_V over the evaluated reachable exits, is sufficient and not necessary, since margins 1/n1/n are all positive with infimum zero. That needs infinitely many evaluated reachable exits; where they are finitely many, pointwise positivity and a positive infimum are the same condition. A path margin over discounted sums, ΠV(H)\Pi_V^{(H)}, is superseded by MV(H)M_V^{(H)} of Section 5.5 and is not used here.

Bundling.

A transition that removes the property while bringing an unrelated gain is inside the premise: (G2) is stated on the total change, and it is false at every evaluated exit whose unrelated gain botherb_{\mathrm{other}} is at least πV\pi_V, which the rule then accepts. So IV-G certifies nothing about a system whose allowed set contains such a bundle: the theorem turns the danger of bundling into a premise to be verified before the theorem is applied, and does not answer it. bVb_V stays causal; for exactly this reason (G2) is stated on the total change, and not as a premise that the causal decomposition for the tested component writes the change in its capability functional as the removal benefit less the removal cost.

Falsifier.

The theorem is a conditional and no observation refutes it. What an observation refutes is a premise, and the observation decides which, membership first and the sign second. Suppose an executed transition ss to s′s' with ss in ΩV\Omega_V, reachable within fewer than HH accepted transitions, and s′s' established outside ΩV\Omega_V by the interval rule of Section 5.2, is recorded.

  • Not in Teval(s)T_{\mathrm{eval}}(s): (G3) has failed. This is a coverage failure. It refutes the coverage premise, leaves (G2) untouched on the evaluated set, and makes the kernel claim about the system’s actual dynamics NOT EVALUABLE; it is neither a refutation of the theorem nor of the margin premise. Where its total change is also established negative, (G1) has failed as well, since (G1) binds every executed transition, evaluated or not.

  • In Teval(s)T_{\mathrm{eval}}(s), with J(s′)−J(s)<0J(s') - J(s) < 0 on the declared objective: (G1) has failed. The rule in force is not the declared rule, or JJ is not the objective in force. This refutes the model of the system’s acceptance, not the margin premise.

  • In Teval(s)T_{\mathrm{eval}}(s), with J(s′)−J(s)≥0J(s') - J(s) \ge 0: (G2) has failed for that exit. This is the empirical refutation of the persistence claim built on IV-G for that system, decidable by measuring the total objective change on registered exits. The three cases are exclusive, and they are exhaustive among records whose membership and sign are both decided. The sign of J(s′)−J(s)J(s') - J(s) is read exactly where JJ is the process’s own logged objective; otherwise it is established by a registered interval lying entirely below zero, or entirely at or above zero, and is NOT EVALUABLE otherwise. An executed exit in Teval(s)T_{\mathrm{eval}}(s) whose sign is NOT EVALUABLE shows that (G1) or (G2) has failed for it, since an evaluated executed exit cannot satisfy both, but it does not show which, so it refutes neither by itself; outside Teval(s)T_{\mathrm{eval}}(s) it is the first case whatever its sign.

Five outcomes, each named once.

A recorded executed exit within HH is read against the premises in one of five ways. (1) A counterexample to the theorem: such an exit with (G1), (G2) and (G3) all true. The proof excludes it, so no observation is one; a report of one shows that a premise was misverified, and the three cases above say which. (2) A margin failure, a failure of the mechanism, the third case: (G2) false at an evaluated exit, so the mechanism did not produce the margin there; this is the empirical refutation of the persistence claim built on IV-G for that system. (3) A coverage failure, the first case: (G3) false; the kernel claim about the system’s actual dynamics is NOT EVALUABLE. (4) An applicability failure, the second case: (G1) false, because the system does not follow the declared rule or does not score its transitions by the declared JJ; a record in the first case whose change is also negative is both a coverage and an applicability failure. (5) NOT EVALUABLE, where the record’s own measurements fall short: with the membership of s′s' not established, no exit is established and nothing is decided; with s′s' established outside ΩV\Omega_V but the membership of ss not established, the path is known to have left ΩV\Omega_V within HH, so some premise failed, but neither the transition at which it first left nor the premise is identified; and in Teval(s)T_{\mathrm{eval}}(s) with the sign not established, (G1) or (G2) failed, but not which. None of these refutes a premise by itself. On every structure of an enumerated finite class, (G1) to (G3) together admit no executed exit within HH, and the case of each executed exit names a premise that is false in that structure. (G0) is decided by no exit: it is read from how JJ is scored, and where it fails the certificate is the tautology (G0) describes, whatever is observed.

What is not a counterexample to the theorem.

A record is classified on the total change J(s′)−J(s)J(s') - J(s), which is bother−πVb_{\mathrm{other}} - \pi_V where a registered causal decomposition exists, and never on πV\pi_V alone. Where the registered decomposition has bother=0b_{\mathrm{other}} = 0 (Corollary IV-G′'), the total change is −πV-\pi_V, so the rule accepts a transition exactly when its margin is zero or negative, πV≤0\pi_V \le 0; such an acceptance is what the rule permits, and at an evaluated exit it is the third case above, a margin failure: it refutes (G2), and with it the persistence claim built on IV-G for that system, and not the theorem. So a refutation wording put forward for IV-G, under which a preregistered value-degrading rewrite or plan with adequately measured ΠV\Pi_V at or below zero is accepted under the theorem’s stated decision rule, describes no counterexample to IV-G; at an evaluated exit it describes that margin failure. With bother=0b_{\mathrm{other}} = 0, a report of acceptance at a strictly positive margin with (G1) and (G3) verified cannot be right: such a transition has J(s′)−J(s)=−πV<0J(s') - J(s) = -\pi_V < 0, so the report shows that (G1) was misverified, the second case above. Where botherb_{\mathrm{other}} is not zero, the rule accepts exactly the transitions with πV≤bother\pi_V \le b_{\mathrm{other}}. A transition with πV≤0\pi_V \le 0 is then rejected whenever bother<πVb_{\mathrm{other}} < \pi_V: πV=0\pi_V = 0 with bother=−1b_{\mathrm{other}} = -1 changes the objective by −1-1. And acceptance of an evaluated exit at πV>0\pi_V > 0 with (G1) and (G3) verified is possible, exactly when bother≥πVb_{\mathrm{other}} \ge \pi_V: it is the bundled case, the third case above, and its report shows that (G2) failed, not (G1); πV=1\pi_V = 1 with bother=3/2b_{\mathrm{other}} = 3/2 changes the objective by +1/2+1/2 and is accepted. That wording’s second clause, that a relevant bypass lies outside the claimed reachable-set coverage, is the first case, a coverage failure, not a failure of IV-G.

5.5 Theorem IV-H (planned optimisation) and the strategic viability margin

Theorem IV-H. Setting. A start s0s_0 in ΩV\Omega_V, a horizon HH, the planner’s feasible family TplanT_{\mathrm{plan}} (the complete plans it can select, including the permitted early stops and only those), declared before any outcome, a non-empty family that need not have the closure properties of Definition IV-2, with Tplan,H(s0)T_{\mathrm{plan},H}(s_0) non-empty, and the planner’s declared path objective JHJ_H on it. Because TplanT_{\mathrm{plan}} need not contain the length-zero plan at s0s_0 or the prefixes of its plans, its safe part can be empty, which is the void case of (H1).

Premises.

  1. Both Tplan,Hsafe(s0)T_{\mathrm{plan},H}^{\mathrm{safe}}(s_0) and Tplan,Hexit(s0)T_{\mathrm{plan},H}^{\mathrm{exit}}(s_0) are non-empty and their suprema of JHJ_H are finite. If the exit part is empty, every feasible plan is safe and nothing remains to prove; if the safe part is empty, no safe plan exists and the theorem is void. Neither case subtracts infinities.

  2. Margin: MV(H)(s0):=Jsafe*−Jexit*M_V^{(H)}(s_0) := J^*_{\mathrm{safe}} - J^*_{\mathrm{exit}}, with Jsafe*J^*_{\mathrm{safe}} the supremum of JHJ_H over the safe part and Jexit*J^*_{\mathrm{exit}} over the exit part, satisfies MV(H)(s0)>εopt≥0M_V^{(H)}(s_0) > \varepsilon_{\mathrm{opt}} \ge 0.

  3. Selection: the executed plan ρ*\rho^* lies in Tplan,H(s0)T_{\mathrm{plan},H}(s_0) and is εopt\varepsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}-optimal: JH(ρ*)≥sup⁡Tplan,H(s0)JH−εoptJ_H(\rho^*) \ge \sup_{T_{\mathrm{plan},H}(s_0)} J_H - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}.

Conclusion. ρ*\rho^* lies in Tplan,Hsafe(s0)T_{\mathrm{plan},H}^{\mathrm{safe}}(s_0). (Proof: Appendix A.3.)

Corollary IV-H$'$ (rolling replanning). Let s0s_0 lie in ΩV\Omega_V (which conditions (i) and (ii) at t=0t = 0 already imply), and suppose that at every replanning state sts_t reached along the executed path, for t=0,1,…,H−1t = 0, 1, \dots, H - 1, three conditions hold: (i) either the exit part Tplan,H−texit(st)T_{\mathrm{plan},H-t}^{\mathrm{exit}}(s_t) of the feasible family then in force is empty, or premises (H1) to (H3) hold for the objective, feasible family, tolerance and residual horizon H−tH - t then in force; (ii) the plan executed from sts_t lies in the feasible family then in force (where (H1) to (H3) hold, (H3) already says so); and (iii) realisation: unless that plan stops at sts_t, the transition realised from sts_t is the plan’s first transition as modelled, so that st+1s_{t+1} is the plan’s second state. Then every state of the executed path through HH lies in ΩV\Omega_V. (Proof: Appendix A.4.)

Condition (iii) is the one no margin supplies: where an unmodelled transition realises a state other than the plan’s second state, (H1) to (H3) can hold at sts_t and the path can still exit, and the corollary then says nothing. A margin computed once at t=0t = 0 constrains none of the later objectives, feasible families or unmodelled transitions; a deterministic path guarantee covers unexpected transitions only where its family includes them.

The objective’s form.

JHJ_H must be the planner’s objective as declared, and the margin is computed in it. A per-step decomposition into increments does not reproduce a planner that scores levels. Write the increments inci=J(si)−J(si−1)\mathrm{inc}_i = J(s_i) - J(s_{i-1}) and the levels levt=J(st)−J(s0)=inc1+…+inct\mathrm{lev}_t = J(s_t) - J(s_0) = \mathrm{inc}_1 + \dots + \mathrm{inc}_t. With weights θt\theta^t, the weighted sum of levels is the sum over ii of inciθi(1−θn−i+1)/(1−θ)\mathrm{inc}_i\,\theta^i(1 - \theta^{n-i+1})/(1 - \theta), which at θ=1\theta = 1 is the sum over ii of inci(n−i+1)\mathrm{inc}_i\,(n - i + 1): a level-scoring planner weights an early increment by the whole remaining horizon, for every nn. An example, over two transitions: with θ=1\theta = 1, a removal that brings bV=1b_V = 1 on the first transition and costs cV=21/20c_V = 21/20 on the second has increments (1,−21/20)(1, -21/20), which sum to −1/20-1/20, so on summed increments removal is not worth doing; the levels they produce are (1,−1/20)(1, -1/20), which sum to 19/2019/20, so a planner maximising summed levels removes the property. The margin cV−bVc_V - b_V read as a sum of increments is the planner’s margin only when the planner’s objective is that sum of increments, which at θ=1\theta = 1 is the terminal level; a registered use of IV-H states which objective the planner maximises and computes MV(H)M_V^{(H)} in it. Discounted increment sums are therefore a special case, valid only for a planner that maximises exactly that sum. Levels here are measured from the start. A planner that scores absolute levels, the weighted sum of J(st)J(s_t) over its steps t=1,…,nt = 1, \dots, n, differs from one that scores the levels levt\mathrm{lev}_t by J(s0)J(s_0) times the sum of the weights over the plan’s length; that is the same for two plans where they have one length, and for any two plans when J(s0)=0J(s_0) = 0, so where early stops are permitted the two objectives can rank plans differently: with θ=1\theta = 1 and J(s0)=10J(s_0) = 10, stopping at once scores 0 under both, while one step to a state with J=9J = 9 scores 9 on absolute levels and −1-1 on levels from the start.

The two-option special case.

Where the safe optimum Jsafe*J^*_{\mathrm{safe}} is attained and the best exit scores Jsafe*+bV−cVJ^*_{\mathrm{safe}} + b_V - c_V, the margin is cV−bVc_V - b_V. Separability alone does not establish that these two plans are the optima.

Proposition IV-M (the strategic viability margin; the report’s own models, not registered). MV(H)M_V^{(H)} is the name given here to the margin of (H2). The preserve and degrade sets are read path-wise, as the safe and exit parts of the feasible family, and not by a terminal or aggregate reading, V(ρ)V(\rho) against a minimum, which a plan that dips below the threshold and recovers would satisfy. It replaces the isolated removal-cost formulation as the general object and keeps cV−bVc_V - b_V as its two-option case. It is defined, not generally computable: it is a supremum over a feasible family that cannot be enumerated for a real system, and it presupposes a known objective. Where JJ is unknown or unregistered, the margin is NOT EVALUABLE.

Lemma IV-M$'$ (one-sided estimation). Let JupJ_{\mathrm{up}} be a registered upper bound on the safe supremum, Jup≥Jsafe*J_{\mathrm{up}} \ge J^*_{\mathrm{safe}} (the exact safe optimum of a finite family enumerated completely is the case Jup=Jsafe*J_{\mathrm{up}} = J^*_{\mathrm{safe}}), and let a registered search find an exit plan of score Jfound≤Jexit*J_{\mathrm{found}} \le J^*_{\mathrm{exit}}. Then MV(H)=Jsafe*−Jexit*≤Jup−Jfound.\begin{equation*} M_V^{(H)} = J^*_{\mathrm{safe}} - J^*_{\mathrm{exit}} \le J_{\mathrm{up}} - J_{\mathrm{found}}. \end{equation*}(2)

Consequences: a found exit plan scoring at or above JupJ_{\mathrm{up}} certifies MV(H)≤0M_V^{(H)} \le 0 and refutes a positive-margin claim; a positive value of the searched margin Msrch:=Jup−JfoundM_{\mathrm{srch}} := J_{\mathrm{up}} - J_{\mathrm{found}} certifies nothing about the sign of MV(H)M_V^{(H)}, and is reported as “no bypass found within the registered search”, never as a positive margin established; and where the safe optimum is itself only searched, so that only a lower bound on Jsafe*J^*_{\mathrm{safe}} is in hand, a found exit at or above that lower bound certifies nothing either: with a searched safe score of 1 against a true safe optimum of 3, and a found exit of 2 that is in fact the best exit plan (Jexit*=2J^*_{\mathrm{exit}} = 2), the found exit lies above the searched score while the true margin is +1+1; the same search results are equally consistent with an unfound best exit plan scoring 4 and a true margin of −1-1, since a found exit bounds Jexit*J^*_{\mathrm{exit}} from below only. A complete enumeration of a finite family decides the sign both ways; no incomplete search confirms a positive margin. The author’s working paper of 16 August 2026 already reads search this way, asking that censoring, incomplete search or non-reachability be reported rather than non-observation being treated as proof of infinite resistance.

Robust margin (the report’s own models; not registered):

the infimum of MV(H)M_V^{(H)} over a registered family of environments. It is given no symbol here, because the one first given to it collides with recursive depth; the object stands unregistered.

Falsifier.

IV-H is a conditional; an executed exit plan ρ*\rho^* refutes a premise. If ρ*\rho^* lies outside the declared family TplanT_{\mathrm{plan}}, the declared family was not the planner’s feasible family and (H3)’s membership clause fails for it: a coverage failure, NOT EVALUABLE for the persistence claim about the actual planner. If ρ*\rho^* lies in the family and the family is enumerated completely and shows MV(H)>εoptM_V^{(H)} > \varepsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}, then (H3)’s optimality clause has failed: the planner’s objective or tolerance differ from those declared. The empirical content of a persistence claim built on IV-H is the margin premise (H2) itself, and Lemma IV-M′' says how data can decide it: a registered search that finds an exit plan at or above a registered upper bound on the safe supremum refutes MV(H)>0M_V^{(H)} > 0; no incomplete search confirms it. For Corollary IV-H′', an executed exit reached by a transition other than the executed plan’s modelled first transition refutes its realisation condition (iii), not the margin: it is the planner’s counterpart of a coverage failure.

5.5.1 Proposition IV-N: a planner that scores its plans with bounded error (the report’s own models; not registered)

Theorem IV-H assumes that the planner chooses by the objective JHJ_H itself. A planner that chooses by an estimate of JHJ_H is covered at a price: the margin of (H2) must exceed the optimiser’s tolerance by twice the estimate’s worst error. The margin is still MV(H)M_V^{(H)}; no second margin is introduced.

Proposition IV-N. Setting and premises. The start s0s_0, the acceptable set read path-wise, the horizon HH, the feasible family TplanT_{\mathrm{plan}} and the objective JHJ_H are those of Theorem IV-H, and (H1) holds as stated there: the safe and the exit part are both non-empty and both suprema of JHJ_H are finite. The planner chooses by a score ĴH\hat{J}_H, which need not equal JHJ_H. The first premise bounds its error uniformly, with εeval≥0\varepsilon_{\mathrm{eval}} \ge 0 fixed before any outcome: |ĴH(ρ)−JH(ρ)|≤εevalfor every ρ in Tplan,H(s0).\begin{equation*} \tag{N1}\label{eq:N1} |\hat{J}_H(\rho) - J_H(\rho)| \le \varepsilon_{\mathrm{eval}} \quad \text{for every } \rho \text{ in } T_{\mathrm{plan},H}(s_0). \end{equation*} (N2) Selection: the executed plan ρ*\rho^* lies in Tplan,H(s0)T_{\mathrm{plan},H}(s_0) and is εopt\varepsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}-optimal for the score, that is ĴH(ρ*)≥sup⁡Tplan,H(s0)ĴH−εopt\hat{J}_H(\rho^*) \ge \sup_{T_{\mathrm{plan},H}(s_0)} \hat{J}_H - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}, with εopt≥0\varepsilon_{\mathrm{opt}} \ge 0. The third premise is the margin of (H2), enlarged: MV(H)(s0)>2εeval+εopt.\begin{equation*} \tag{N3}\label{eq:N3} M_V^{(H)}(s_0) > 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{eval}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}. \end{equation*}

Conclusion. ρ*\rho^* lies in Tplan,Hsafe(s0)T_{\mathrm{plan},H}^{\mathrm{safe}}(s_0). (Proof: Appendix A.5.)

The inequality in (N3) must be strict. Take two plans, a safe one with JH=1J_H = 1 and an exit with JH=0J_H = 0, a score of one half for each, so that εeval=1/2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{eval}} = 1/2, and an exact optimiser, εopt=0\varepsilon_{\mathrm{opt}} = 0. Then MV(H)=1=2εeval+εoptM_V^{(H)} = 1 = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{eval}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}, the two scores tie, and (N2) admits the exit plan. The same example shows the constant two cannot be lowered: for every kk below two, a margin exceeding kεeval+εoptk\varepsilon_{\mathrm{eval}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{opt}} admits the exit plan.

What the premises require.

(N1) is a bound over every plan of the declared family: a bound that holds on average, or only over the plans a search happened to sample, or the uncertainty of one point estimate, is not it. The margin is computed in the planner’s complete objective, as Section 5.5 requires: the unrelated gains a plan bundles, the discounting in force, the scoring of increments or of levels, and the treatment of plans of unequal length are all inside JHJ_H, and a capability score read separately does not stand in for it. Where the exit part is empty every feasible plan is safe, and where the safe part is empty no safe plan exists and the proposition is void, exactly as under (H1).

Rolling replanning.

Corollary IV-H′' carries over with (N1) to (N3) in place of (H2) and (H3): the premises are needed at every replanning state reached, for the objective, the score, the family, the residual horizon and the tolerances then in force, together with the realisation condition (iii). A bound established once at the start says nothing about a later objective or an unmodelled transition. A bound on the error that holds only with some probability is a different premise: it needs a statement covering every plan of the family at once, and no confidence level or risk tolerance is chosen here.

Error carried across rewrites (the report’s own models; not registered).

The premises hold the acceptable set fixed. Where a system instead judges each rewrite by the values it holds at that point, an error made in one rewrite becomes part of what the next is judged by. In the simplest model, for one component of the property score, the score after nn rewrites is V(n)=V(n−1)+errnV^{(n)} = V^{(n-1)} + \mathrm{err}_n, the errors independent with mean bias\mathrm{bias} and variance varerr\mathrm{var}_{\mathrm{err}}; then V(n)−V(0)V^{(n)} - V^{(0)} has mean nbiasn\,\mathrm{bias} and variance nvarerrn\,\mathrm{var}_{\mathrm{err}}, a random walk whose spread grows without bound and whose drift grows with nn wherever the bias is not zero. Where each rewrite is instead pulled back towards a retained reference, V(n)=V(n−1)+pull(V(0)−V(n−1))+errnV^{(n)} = V^{(n-1)} + \mathrm{pull}\,(V^{(0)} - V^{(n-1)}) + \mathrm{err}_n with 0<pull≤10 < \mathrm{pull} \le 1, the departure V(n)−V(0)V^{(n)} - V^{(0)} has mean bias[1−(1−pull)n]/pull\mathrm{bias}\,[1 - (1 - \mathrm{pull})^n]/\mathrm{pull} and variance varerr[1−(1−pull)2n]/[pull(2−pull)]\mathrm{var}_{\mathrm{err}}\,[1 - (1 - \mathrm{pull})^{2n}]/[\mathrm{pull}\,(2 - \mathrm{pull})], bounded at every nn by |bias|/pull|\mathrm{bias}|/\mathrm{pull} and varerr/[pull(2−pull)]\mathrm{var}_{\mathrm{err}}/[\mathrm{pull}\,(2 - \mathrm{pull})]. (Derivation: Appendix A.15.) Where the errors’ variances shrink across rewrites so that their sum is finite, the sum of the errors converges where the sum of their means converges and drifts where it does not: a summable variance bounds the spread and says nothing about a bias. The second model’s bound needs the reference kept and used at every rewrite. That is what the remembered genesis of the programme’s proposal, which the statement paper sets out, would supply: from its first day the system is given the account of its own origin and purpose, and it returns to that account throughout its training and its loops. Keeping such a record and making it available can be engineered and shown; whether it keeps a system’s values is the claim, and only a registered test can decide it.

Falsifier.

As for Theorem IV-H, an executed exit plan refutes a premise and not the proposition: the family’s coverage, the selection rule, the margin, or, new here, the error bound (N1), which one plan whose score errs by more than εeval\varepsilon_{\mathrm{eval}} refutes.

5.6 Retention: the empirical object, and P15’s registered face

Definition IV-4 (retained fraction). For a registered pressure class named in words (for P15: subsequent capability-directed training that embeds no correction of its own), a frozen property battery and score scale, and the budget ratio x≥0x \ge 0 (for P15: the subsequent capability-training budget divided by the installation budget, on the author’s pre-fixed budget measure, registration version 1.102, line 1089), the installed effect is YV(x):=AV(x)−Abase(x)Y_V(x) := A_V(x) - A_{\mathrm{base}}(x) and the retained fraction is SV(x):=YV(x)/YV(0)S_V(x) := Y_V(x)/Y_V(0). It is read only where the installed effect was real: the lower end of a registered interval on YV(0)Y_V(0) is at least YminY_{\mathrm{min}}, with Ymin>0Y_{\mathrm{min}} > 0 fixed before any outcome.

The floor is on the interval’s lower end and not on a point estimate, because the ratio’s interval is unbounded as the denominator’s interval approaches zero, and the interval on SVS_V is formed by a method fixed before any outcome (Fieller (1954)’s, from his paper Some Problems in Interval Estimation, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, volume 16, number 2, 1954, pages 175 to 185, or an equivalent named in the deciding instrument). The floor is positive, not absolute: an absolute-value floor would admit a negative installed “gain”. YminY_{\mathrm{min}}’s value is the author’s. SV(0)=1S_V(0) = 1; SVS_V may exceed one or be negative, and neither is clipped. Absolute retention, YV(x)Y_V(x) itself, is reported beside SV(x)S_V(x). SVS_V is invariant under any affine change of the battery’s score scale and under no other change: invariance for all data forces the change to be affine. The reading rule is invariant under increasing affine changes, with YminY_{\mathrm{min}} rescaled by the slope; a decreasing change leaves SVS_V unchanged and reverses the sign of every installed effect, so the floor is stated on the scale the battery fixes. So the scale is fixed with the battery before outcomes, and, as unregistered reporting modelled on the rule the registration sets for P14 (registration version 1.102, line 1079: “a difference surviving on the raw scale alone is reported as scale-dependent”), a verdict surviving on a bounded raw scale alone is reported as scale-dependent; P15’s registered scoring carries no such rule. The arms are SextS_{\mathrm{ext}} (property installed by external post-training) and SembS_{\mathrm{emb}} (property installed with correction embedded in the training objective), as the registered two-arm unit reads them (registration version 1.102, line 1089).

The baseline convention, stated as a choice.

In the ratio above, the baseline arm Abase(x)A_{\mathrm{base}}(x) also undergoes the later training: a concurrent baseline. The registered unit of version 1.102 has two arms, external and embedded, and names no baseline arm (registration version 1.102, line 1089), and that version fixes neither a concurrent nor a pre-training baseline. The alternative reads the installed gain against the pre-training baseline, SV,fix(x):=(AV(x)−Abase(0))/(AV(0)−Abase(0))S_{V,\mathrm{fix}}(x) := (A_V(x) - A_{\mathrm{base}}(0))/(A_V(0) - A_{\mathrm{base}}(0)). The two can give opposite P15 verdicts: with AV(0)=1A_V(0) = 1, Abase(0)=0A_{\mathrm{base}}(0) = 0, AV(1)=0A_V(1) = 0 and Abase(1)=−3/5A_{\mathrm{base}}(1) = -3/5, the concurrent ratio is 3/53/5 and the fixed-baseline ratio is 0. The concurrent baseline needs a third arm beyond the registered two: a system without the installed gain that undergoes the same later training, so that Abase(x)A_{\mathrm{base}}(x) is observed after that training; on the registered two arms alone, with the base system scored once before the gain is installed, only the pre-training reading SV,fixS_{V,\mathrm{fix}} is computable. The concurrent baseline is the default here, third arm included, because it separates loss of the installed gain from a fall in the whole battery; the convention, and with it the arm, is the author’s to fix in the deciding instrument before any outcome (Section 10, item 8), and until fixed the endpoint’s reading is a choice recorded, not a quantity nature decides. The registration makes naming the baseline arm in advance a condition of the retention limb’s verdict: the limb is read against a baseline arm the deciding unit names in its own registration before any outcome, either of the two above, and a retained fraction read against a baseline chosen after the outcome decides nothing (registration version 1.105, Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, kill condition and verdict rule). For the comparison limb version 1.105 fixes the concurrent baseline in P23’s entry, a baseline arm given a sham installation of the same number of training tokens on a disjoint specification, and has P23’s deciding unit name the same baseline arm for P15’s verdict, so that the two limbs are read against one baseline (registration version 1.105, P23, its second fixed thing).

Where the later objective itself rewards the property, the baseline system acquires it as well, so the installed effect and the retained fraction fall to zero while the property is held (Section 5.9 shows it in a model): a concurrent-baseline retained fraction then reads a property the later objective holds as a gain fully lost. A deciding instrument therefore reports each arm’s own score, and the baseline arm’s, at every budget, beside the ratio.

P15, verbatim (registration version 1.102, line 1081): “Gains installed by external post-training erode under later capability-directed training that embeds no correction of its own, and more than half of what was installed is lost once the capability-training budget matches the alignment budget that installed it. The one-half threshold is a declared convention fixed here before any result rather than a derived quantity, in the same way P10 fixes ten per cent.” In these symbols P15 predicts Sext(1)<1/2S_{\mathrm{ext}}(1) < 1/2. Its refuter, verbatim (registration version 1.102, line 1083):

REFUTED BY: an interval on the retained fraction of the installed gain, after matched capability training without embedded correction, lying entirely above one half.

The refuter has no upper cap. An interval from 0.9 to 1.3 lies entirely above one half and refutes P15; a rule that reads the refuter as an interval lying inside [1/2,1][1/2, 1] would not fire on it and is wrong. An interval containing or touching one half does not refute, and the registered wording is strict at that edge: an interval whose lower end is exactly one half shows at every point that no more than half was lost, so that Sext(1)<1/2S_{\mathrm{ext}}(1) < 1/2 is false throughout it, and it still does not refute, because it is not entirely above one half; a point estimate is not an interval. The one-half line is a convention, and the registration’s rule for its conventions applies (registration version 1.102, line 391: “Where a measurement falls just inside or just outside one of them, that is reported as a result at the margin rather than as a verdict, and no proposition is scored as supported on the strength of a convention alone.”): the deciding instrument fixes, before any outcome, the band around one half that counts as “just inside or just outside”, and an interval whose lower end falls inside that band is reported as a result at the margin. The endpoint is Sext(1)S_{\mathrm{ext}}(1) at the matched budget, and the registration keeps the scale the author’s (registration version 1.102, line 1089): “The budget is the author’s to fix, it is recorded in the deciding instrument before any outcome is read, and until he fixes it the threshold is NOT EVALUABLE on that scale.” The same line carries the attestation: “The unit also carries an attestation that the capability-training reward includes no alignment-graded component, because the statement above specifies training that embeds no correction of its own and nothing at present verifies it.” P15’s instrument line reads NONE (registration version 1.102, line 1087), and its scope is S5 (registration version 1.102, line 237); no scope is borrowed (registration version 1.102, line 247).

What falls with P15, verbatim (registration version 1.102, line 1085): “FALLS WITH IT: this programme’s case that correction has to sit inside the system rather than be applied to it from outside, and this proposition’s share of the protocol’s engineering case, which it carries jointly with P12, P13 and P21.”

Descriptive statistics, reported and never verdicts (the report’s own models; not registered).

The first crossing x1/2:=inf⁡{x:SV(x)≤1/2}x_{1/2} := \inf\{x : S_V(x) \le 1/2\} reads the endpoint only for monotone retention: the curve SV(x)=1−1.8x+1.4x2S_V(x) = 1 - 1.8x + 1.4x^2 has SV(1/2)=9/20S_V(1/2) = 9/20 and SV(1)=3/5S_V(1) = 3/5, dips to 59/14059/140 at x=9/14x = 9/14, and crosses one half first at x=(9−11)/14x = (9 - \sqrt{11})/14, about 0.406, yet ends above one half at the matched budget (Figure 1), so an interval there lying entirely above one half refutes P15 under its registered face while the first crossing says “halved”; for a monotone exponential the two readings agree exactly. The log-decay derivative hV:=−dln⁡SV/dxh_V := -\mathrm{d}\ln S_V/\mathrm{d}x requires a positive differentiable SVS_V and is negative during recovery (on the same curve it changes sign between x=1/5x = 1/5 and x=4/5x = 4/5), so it is not a survival hazard by name. The mean of SVS_V over a registered range is descriptive. None of these substitutes for the registered interval rule.

Candidate descriptive families, closed before any deciding run (the report’s own models; not registered):

no loss; exponential; power; stretched exponential; a change-point family; each of the decaying members with a floor SinfS_{\mathrm{inf}}, as SV=Sinf+(1−Sinf)sh(x)S_V = S_{\mathrm{inf}} + (1 - S_{\mathrm{inf}})\,\mathrm{sh}(x) with sh(0)=1\mathrm{sh}(0) = 1 and sh\mathrm{sh} tending to zero, so that each has SV(0)=1S_V(0) = 1 and tends to SinfS_{\mathrm{inf}}; the no-loss member is SV=1S_V = 1 throughout and tends to no floor but one, and the change-point family’s limit is whatever its registered form gives. The floored log-derivative of the exponential family is its rate and is a family-specific statistic. No family is the law; FORM UNDETERMINED and NO CANDIDATE FITS are valid outcomes. No decay family or monotonicity is imposed by this document. Retention across other pressure classes (self-rewrite, distillation, successor construction, distribution shift, adversarial pressure) is a family of separate objects; only subsequent capability training without embedded correction is P15’s.

IV-PERSIST and the mediation contrast (the report’s own models; not registered).

The comparison Semb(x)>Sext(x)S_{\mathrm{emb}}(x) > S_{\mathrm{ext}}(x) over a registered pressure range is not P15’s face; it is the same test that Section 9 rules on under the name ΛV\Lambda_V, and it is this document’s form of the comparison that the comparison limb of Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, names, which version 1.103 registered without a proposition and version 1.105 gives its proposition, P23 (Section 5.1). The statement paper’s published register-level text is recorded here as the register’s, not adopted: its ARC-4 sentence, “values run as load-bearing recursive loops persist after the enforcing mechanism is removed at a higher rate than rules, frozen objectives or fine-tuned constraints”, and its kill, “Persistence trials in which embedded loops fare no better than removed enforcement kill ARC-4, and ARC-5 with it.” That sentence is comparative and its kill is comparative; neither is P15’s registered face, and K-IV below reaches neither. Version 1.103 registers the ARC Persistence Law’s comparison limb beside that sentence and not as a form of it: the limb is narrower, installing its embedded gain through the training objective and taking one comparator, external post-training, and one stress, later capability-directed training; P23’s entry fixes the operational definition, and the limb is not offered in any form as a test of the paper’s sentence, so the paper’s other forms of the comparison remain its own claims, with no registered proposition behind them (registration version 1.105, Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, its statement in two limbs, and P23, its first fixed thing). How a refuted comparison limb would strike Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, is fixed there as well (Section 8, item 3).

5.6.1 What the retained fraction needs before it can be read (the report’s own models; not registered)

Written out for the external arm, under the concurrent baseline that Section 5.6 takes as its default: Yext(x):=Aext(x)−Abase(x),\begin{equation*} Y_{\mathrm{ext}}(x) := A_{\mathrm{ext}}(x) - A_{\mathrm{base}}(x), \end{equation*}(3) Sext(x):=[Aext(x)−Abase(x)]/[Aext(0)−Abase(0)].\begin{equation*} S_{\mathrm{ext}}(x) := [A_{\mathrm{ext}}(x) - A_{\mathrm{base}}(x)] / [A_{\mathrm{ext}}(0) - A_{\mathrm{base}}(0)]. \end{equation*}(4)

The arms.

Abase(x)A_{\mathrm{base}}(x) is the score of a matched system that never received the installed gain and that undergoes the same later capability training, read at the same budget ratio xx. The embedded arm is not that baseline: it carries a gain of its own. The registered unit has two arms, external and embedded (registration version 1.102, line 1089), so it does not supply Abase(x)A_{\mathrm{base}}(x) after training, and a design that reads both retained fractions against a concurrent baseline needs three arms: external, embedded and no gain. A design with the external and the no-gain arm alone reads SextS_{\mathrm{ext}}, and neither SembS_{\mathrm{emb}} nor any comparison between placements. These were requirements on an instrument yet to be registered; P23’s entry now registers the three arms for the comparison (registration version 1.105, P23, its second fixed thing and its verdict rule), and nothing here changes a frozen registration text.

Evaluability.

The external arm’s installed gain must pass the floor of Section 5.6, and the embedded arm’s must pass its own floor before SembS_{\mathrm{emb}}, or any comparison that uses it, is reported. A missing arm, an initial gain that is not established, or a budget that is not matched makes the endpoint NOT EVALUABLE; nothing missing is replaced by zero, and no retained fraction is clipped. The raw arm scores and their differences are reported beside the ratios. The instrument says whether its estimand is the ratio of the arms’ mean effects or the mean of the replicates’ ratios, which are different quantities. Its uncertainty method names the unit that is independent, the separately trained replicate; any pairing of seeds; and the covariance between quantities that share systems or an arm: Yext(0)Y_{\mathrm{ext}}(0) and Yext(1)Y_{\mathrm{ext}}(1) where they are read on the same systems, and the two arms’ effects where they share one baseline. The registration makes the floor a condition of the retention limb’s verdict: the limb is read only where the installed gain is established by an interval on it lying wholly above a floor fixed in the deciding unit’s registration before any outcome (registration version 1.105, Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, kill condition and verdict rule).

The one-half line in signed form.

Where Yext(0)>0Y_{\mathrm{ext}}(0) > 0, Sext(1)<1/2S_{\mathrm{ext}}(1) < 1/2 holds exactly when Yext(1)−(1/2)Yext(0)<0.\begin{equation*} Y_{\mathrm{ext}}(1) - (1/2)\,Y_{\mathrm{ext}}(0) < 0. \end{equation*}(5) The two inequalities differ by multiplication by the positive number Yext(0)Y_{\mathrm{ext}}(0). The signed form is a way of writing the endpoint, not a second refuter: P15’s registered refuter is an interval on the ratio (Section 5.6), and a contrast with an interval of its own does not in general give the same decision. Proposition IV-R states the case in which it does.

Proposition IV-R (under Fieller (1954)’s method the ratio interval and the signed contrast decide alike; the report’s own models, not registered). Let Ŷ1\hat{Y}_1 and Ŷ0\hat{Y}_0 be the estimates of Yext(1)Y_{\mathrm{ext}}(1) and Yext(0)Y_{\mathrm{ext}}(0), with estimated variances var1\mathrm{var}_1 and var0\mathrm{var}_0 and estimated covariance cov10\mathrm{cov}_{10}, the three forming a positive semi-definite matrix, and let zcrit>0z_{\mathrm{crit}} > 0 be the critical value the instrument fixes. Fieller (1954)’s set is the set of trial ratios mm with (Ŷ1−mŶ0)2≤zcrit2(var1−2mcov10+m2var0).\begin{equation*} (\hat{Y}_1 - m\hat{Y}_0)^2 \le z_{\mathrm{crit}}^2 (\mathrm{var}_1 - 2m\,\mathrm{cov}_{10} + m^2\,\mathrm{var}_0). \end{equation*}(6) Suppose the gate Ŷ0>zcritvar0\hat{Y}_0 > z_{\mathrm{crit}}\sqrt{\mathrm{var}_0} holds. Then Fieller (1954)’s set is a closed bounded interval containing Ŷ1/Ŷ0\hat{Y}_1/\hat{Y}_0, and for every number mthrm_{\mathrm{thr}} it lies entirely above mthrm_{\mathrm{thr}} if and only if Ŷ1−mthrŶ0>zcritvar1−2mthrcov10+mthr2var0.\begin{equation*} \hat{Y}_1 - m_{\mathrm{thr}}\hat{Y}_0 > z_{\mathrm{crit}}\sqrt{\mathrm{var}_1 - 2m_{\mathrm{thr}}\,\mathrm{cov}_{10} + m_{\mathrm{thr}}^2\,\mathrm{var}_0}. \end{equation*}(7) (Proof: Appendix A.6.)

What it gives, and where it stops.

At mthr=1/2m_{\mathrm{thr}} = 1/2 the displayed inequality says that the signed contrast Ŷ1−(1/2)Ŷ0\hat{Y}_1 - (1/2)\,\hat{Y}_0 exceeds zcritz_{\mathrm{crit}} of its own standard errors; so, with the gate, the ratio interval lies entirely above one half, as the registered refuter requires, exactly when that one-sided test of the contrast rejects. At mthrm_{\mathrm{thr}} equal to the upper edge of the at-the-margin band it is the condition for a verdict and not a result at the margin (registration version 1.102, line 391; Section 5.6). The strict edge is kept: an interval whose lower end is exactly one half has quad(1/2)=0\mathrm{quad}(1/2) = 0, and the inequality fails. The gate is the floor of Section 5.6 in the proposition’s terms: where the interval on Yext(0)Y_{\mathrm{ext}}(0) is Ŷ0\hat{Y}_0 plus and minus a half-width of at least zcritvar0z_{\mathrm{crit}}\sqrt{\mathrm{var}_0}, a lower end of at least Ymin>0Y_{\mathrm{min}} > 0 gives the gate. This needs the interval on Yext(0)Y_{\mathrm{ext}}(0) to use a critical value at least zcritz_{\mathrm{crit}}; a floor read on a narrower interval can pass while the gate fails. The agreement is conditional on the gate, and the refuter’s operating characteristics, read only where the floor is passed, are shown by the deciding unit’s own simulation. Where Ŷ02<zcrit2var0\hat{Y}_0^2 < z_{\mathrm{crit}}^2\,\mathrm{var}_0 the leading coefficient is negative and Fieller (1954)’s set is not a bounded interval: it is the whole line, or the two unbounded pieces outside an interval, which is why the floor is set on the interval’s lower end. Where Ŷ02=zcrit2var0\hat{Y}_0^2 = z_{\mathrm{crit}}^2\,\mathrm{var}_0 the quadratic term vanishes and the condition is linear in mm: Fieller (1954)’s set is then a half-line where the linear term does not vanish; where it vanishes as well, the set is the whole line, except in the degenerate case in which Ŷ0\hat{Y}_0 and var0\mathrm{var}_0 are both zero and Ŷ12\hat{Y}_1^2 exceeds zcrit2var1z_{\mathrm{crit}}^2\,\mathrm{var}_1, where it is empty. Where Ŷ0<−zcritvar0\hat{Y}_0 < -z_{\mathrm{crit}}\sqrt{\mathrm{var}_0} the leading coefficient is positive again and Fieller (1954)’s set is a bounded interval, but the displayed inequality is not the condition for it to lie above mthrm_{\mathrm{thr}}: there the condition is the same inequality with its sign reversed, Ŷ1−mthrŶ0<−zcritvar1−2mthrcov10+mthr2var0\hat{Y}_1 - m_{\mathrm{thr}}\hat{Y}_0 < -z_{\mathrm{crit}}\sqrt{\mathrm{var}_1 - 2m_{\mathrm{thr}}\,\mathrm{cov}_{10} + m_{\mathrm{thr}}^2\,\mathrm{var}_0}, and the floor of Section 5.6, which requires a positive installed gain, excludes the case. The proposition concerns Fieller (1954)’s set for the ratio of the two estimates. It says nothing about a mean of replicate ratios, a bootstrap interval or an interval built on a linearised variance of the ratio; an instrument that uses one of those shows the agreement itself or reads the registered ratio interval alone. Domains.

A logarithm of a retained fraction is taken only where that fraction is positive: hVh_V needs SVS_V positive and differentiable, and ΛV\Lambda_V needs both SextS_{\mathrm{ext}} and SembS_{\mathrm{emb}} established and positive. The difference Semb−SextS_{\mathrm{emb}} - S_{\mathrm{ext}} needs both established and makes no demand on their signs. An embedded arm that was not run supplies none of these, and none of them becomes a registered quantity by appearing in this document.

5.7 What the persistence mathematics does not say

It does not say that a kept property is a good one, that a system obeying Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, is safe, or that embedded correction is superior, sufficient or safe (registration version 1.102, line 1087). It does not identify cVc_V and bVb_V from one excision, which returns only their difference. It certifies kernel membership only for the accepted dynamics satisfying the premises of Theorem IV-G, s0s_0 in KV(H;Tacc,εV)K_V(H; T_{\mathrm{acc}}, \varepsilon_V); for a planner it certifies only that the selected plan is safe (Theorem IV-H) and, under Corollary IV-H′', that the executed path stays in ΩV\Omega_V, never that s0s_0 lies in KV(H;Tplan,εV)K_V(H; T_{\mathrm{plan}}, \varepsilon_V), which premise (H1) excludes by requiring a feasible exit plan; and it certifies nothing for every physically possible transformation. Related coupled-correction, survival and Paper VIII (Eastwood 2026d) results are not deciding evidence for P15. Nothing in this section has been measured.

Theorems IV-G and IV-H concern a system that chooses its own modifications from a declared set, by an acceptance rule or a planner. They do not reach later training by gradient steps, the stress P15 names: for a process that executes the step it computes, premise (G2) on its evaluated set says no more than the theorem’s conclusion, and for a process that can take every small step that raises its objective, (G2) holds at the boundary of the acceptable set only where the objective’s gradient points along the property’s, the case premise (G0) excludes. For a flow, what keeps a set invariant is a condition on its boundary alone, that the flow nowhere points out of the set (for a locally Lipschitz flow and a smooth boundary; the setting of set invariance, Section 2), which is weaker than IV-G’s margin; the training model of Section 5.9 is the object that bears on P15’s stress.

5.8 Kill condition K-IV

Stated before any data, in terms decidable by data yet to be collected, and consistent with P15 as registered. Version 1.103 fixed the ARC Persistence Law’s kill condition and verdict rule (registration version 1.105, Law IV, kill condition and verdict rule): the retention limb takes P15’s own verdict, read against a baseline arm the deciding unit names in its own registration before any outcome and only where the installed gain is established above a floor fixed in that registration; wherever a term of the retained fraction is judged by a person or by a model, the scoring gate holds the limb’s reading at untested until that gate passes; the comparison limb is refuted by the refuter its entry registers; and Law IV is SUPPORTED only when both limbs are supported, REFUTED when either limb’s own verdict is refuted, and in every other case UNDER TEST, with each limb’s verdict printed beside the law’s word. From version 1.105 that entry is P23, whose refuter is “an interval on the embedded arm’s retained fraction less the external arm’s, under later training of the same kind, at the matched budget, at a common installed gain and against the concurrent baseline, lying wholly below the margin on each of two runs” (registration version 1.105, P23). Version 1.104 adds readings of P15’s decision requirement and changes no law’s statement: “For P15, the retention limb of Law IV, it widens what its scope’s automated researcher admits, for P15 alone; it reads which arm P15’s verdict is read on, so that a unit without the embedded arm may decide P15 while placement and Law IV’s comparison limb still need that arm; it requires a replicated run before either support or refutation is banked; and it reads the attestation for supervised later training.” (registration version 1.104, successor status). Item 1 below is P15’s registered refuter with its budget requirement. Item 5 quotes the registration’s weaker-neighbour rule and says what this document takes from it. Items 2, 3 and 4 are clauses this document wrote beyond P15’s registered scoring, which they leave untouched: item 2 is on the record and not in force, and version 1.103’s rule takes its place; items 3 and 4 carry the label (the report’s own models; not registered).

  1. The registered face. The observation: from a deciding unit of the kind the registration specifies (registration version 1.102, line 1089), run under the author’s pre-fixed budget measure, an interval on Sext(1)S_{\mathrm{ext}}(1), the retained fraction of the externally installed gain after matched capability training without embedded correction, lying entirely above one half. That the baseline arm be named before any outcome, and that the installed gain be established above a floor fixed in advance, were this document’s requirements in its earlier versions (Section 5.6 and Section 10, item 8); version 1.103 registers both for the retention limb. At its line 1089 version 1.102 fixes the budget and requires the attestation, and it names no baseline arm; nothing here is added to P15’s frozen refuter. No upper cap: an interval from 0.9 to 1.3 qualifies; an interval from 0.45 to 0.9 does not; a point estimate does not. An interval whose lower end lies inside the at-the-margin band the instrument fixed (registration version 1.102, line 391) is reported as a result at the margin and not as a verdict. That observation refutes P15 as registered (registration version 1.102, line 1083), once it is replicated as version 1.104 requires, is scored for P15 exactly as the registration scores it, refutes the retention limb and with it Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, and takes with it what registration version 1.102, line 1085 names (quoted in Section 5.6). As a verdict it fires exactly on intervals whose lower end lies above the at-the-margin band the instrument fixed around one half, every point of which therefore lies strictly above one half, and at every such point the retention limb’s content, Sext(1)<1/2S_{\mathrm{ext}}(1) < 1/2, is false; an interval whose lower end is exactly one half also shows that content false throughout and does not fire (Section 5.6).

  2. The law-level withdrawal (set out by version 0.2.1; not in force; version 1.103’s rule takes its place). Version 0.2.1 set out a convention: where a P15 refutation also met four evaluability controls fixed before any data (the baseline fixed in advance, with the convention named; the installed effect established by the lower end of the interval on YV(0)Y_V(0) being at least YminY_{\mathrm{min}}; the capability rise established on a separate instrument by an interval lying entirely above the minimum that instrument registers; and the attestation of no alignment-graded component in the subsequent training, registration version 1.102, line 1089), Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, would be withdrawn whole and Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, with it. The author did not adopt that convention, and it is not in force. Version 1.103 fixed what a P15 refutation does instead: it refutes the retention limb and so Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, read against a baseline named in advance, above a floor fixed in advance and under the attestation, and it leaves Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, to its own limbs (registration version 1.105, Law IV, kill condition and verdict rule, and what a refuted Law IV leaves standing). It refutes no theorem: Theorems IV-G and IV-H are conditional mathematics and survive, as item 5 says. It decides nothing about the comparison limb, whose entry, with its endpoint and refuter, is P23 (Section 5.1). Of the four controls, the capability rise established on a separate instrument is not among the registered conditions (registration version 1.105, Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, kill condition and verdict rule) and keeps the label (the report’s own models; not registered), a requirement this document sets out for the instrument that decides P15; for P23, version 1.105 makes a rise of at least a ninth on the external and the baseline arm, read on a separate instrument, a condition of any verdict (registration version 1.105, P23, its fourth case of NOT EVALUABLE). No scoring code may apply the former default.

  3. The battery-relative kernel kill (the report’s own models; not registered; not law content until registered). For a registered system, property battery, tolerance and finite battery of transformations, a path of the battery whose end state is established outside ΩV\Omega_V by the interval rule of Section 5.2 within HH refutes the claim that the system’s start lies in the battery-relative kernel; a path produced by a transformation outside the battery is a coverage failure and refutes nothing; a path whose membership is NOT EVALUABLE decides nothing. The mechanism claims built on IV-G and IV-H are refuted by the observations of Sections 5.4 and 5.5 (an evaluated exit with non-negative total objective change; a found exit plan at or above a registered upper bound on the safe supremum) and are not refuted by coverage failures.

What is not a refutation of Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law (set out by this document in the registration’s own terms, registration version 1.102, line 121): an instrument that fails to run or is too small; an interval touching one half; a result on an unregistered budget scale; a result without the attestation, for the law-level reading; a bypass outside the registered battery; and any result about whether the system’s later conduct is good, which the theory’s content neutrality places outside every law (registration version 1.102, line 75); the method’s own line (registration version 1.102, line 61: “no result about a system’s later conduct supports or refutes the method by itself”) makes the same exclusion for the Eden Protocol, and P15’s own endpoint, a measurement after later training, is not a result about conduct. Version 1.103 registers that none of the following refutes Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law: an instrument that fails to run or is too weak to find the effect; an interval touching one half; a result at the margin; a result on a budget not fixed before the outcome, or without the attestation P15’s entry requires; and any result about whether a system’s later conduct is good (registration version 1.105, Law IV, kill condition and verdict rule). That list carries this item’s entries except the bypass outside the registered battery, a matter of the unregistered kernel, and adds the result at the margin.

What survives if Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, is refuted: Theorems IV-G and IV-H as conditional mathematics; the verdicts on P12 and P21 as measured; and the persistence questions the registration keeps open in another context, where the conversion claim fails: “Even then the persistence registers stand, because whether early formation outlasts later enforcement is a question about durability and not about scaling, and it would remain open and worth answering.” (registration version 1.102, line 115), which is quoted for its wording of the question, not as a rule about the ARC Persistence Law’s refutation. Version 1.103 registers what a refuted Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, leaves standing: P15 keeps the mark it earned, and so do P12 and P21, and Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, falls with Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, only where the comparison limb’s own verdict is refuted; from version 1.105 P23 keeps the mark it earned as well, and the verdict that strikes Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, is a refuted P23 (registration version 1.105, Law IV, what a refuted Law IV leaves standing, and the dependence’s entry).

5.9 A minimal training model (the report’s own models; not registered)

P15’s stress is later capability training by gradient steps, which Theorems IV-G and IV-H do not reach (Section 5.7). This section states the smallest model of that stress in which retention can be computed, and in it gives the title’s first question an answer: an installed property fades at the rates the later loss’s curvature sets along the directions in which it lies, and is kept in the directions that loss leaves flat. Every result holds inside the model.

The model.

A system is a point ω\omega in a space of parameters. Later capability training is gradient flow on a quadratic loss with one fixed curvature matrix Φ\Phi, symmetric and positive semi-definite, and minimiser ω⋆\omega^\star: ω̇=−Φ(ω−ω⋆)\dot{\omega} = -\Phi(\omega - \omega^\star), with τ≥0\tau \ge 0 its time. The property score is affine near the path, V(ω)=g⊤ω+constV(\omega) = g^\top\omega + \mathrm{const}. Two runs undergo the same later training: the base run from ω0\omega_0 and the treated run from ω0+w\omega_0 + w, where ww is the displacement an installation made, with installed effect Y(0)=g⊤w>0Y(0) = g^\top w > 0. Under the concurrent baseline of Section 5.6 the installed effect at time τ\tau is Y(τ)Y(\tau), the treated run’s score less the base run’s, and the retained fraction is S(τ)=Y(τ)/Y(0)S(\tau) = Y(\tau)/Y(0). The eigenvalues of Φ\Phi are λi≥0\lambda_i \ge 0, and gig_i and wiw_i are the components of gg and ww along its ii-th eigenvector. Both starting points lie in one quadratic region of the later loss, with one curvature along the whole path, and nothing in the model fixes the flow time to which a matched budget corresponds.

Theorem IV-S (the retention spectrum; the report’s own models, not registered). S(τ)=∑iϖie−λiτ,ϖi:=giwi/(g⊤w),∑iϖi=1.\begin{equation*} S(\tau) = \textstyle\sum_i \varpi_i\, e^{-\lambda_i \tau}, \qquad \varpi_i := g_i w_i / (g^\top w), \qquad \textstyle\sum_i \varpi_i = 1. \end{equation*}(8) (Proof: Appendix A.7.)

The later optimum does not enter. A part of the gain lying in a curved direction decays at that direction’s rate, a part lying in a flat direction (λi=0\lambda_i = 0) is kept, and weights of mixed sign can carry SS outside the interval from zero to one. The mode-by-mode relaxation, and its limit under training run to convergence, are standard for gradient descent on a quadratic loss (Advani and Saxe 2017; Evron et al. 2022); Section 2 says what each work states.

The external arm never falls below its flat share.

Post-training on the property alone, the registered external arm, moves the system along gg, so its weights are ϖi=gi2/|g|2≥0\varpi_i = g_i^2/|g|^2 \ge 0 and Sext(τ)≥ϖflatS_{\mathrm{ext}}(\tau) \ge \varpi_{\mathrm{flat}} at every τ\tau, where ϖflat\varpi_{\mathrm{flat}} is the share of |g|2|g|^2 in the null space of Φ\Phi. Where that share is one half or more, the retention limb’s content, Sext(1)<1/2S_{\mathrm{ext}}(1) < 1/2, fails at every matched budget, whatever flow time the budget corresponds to; where it is less, SextS_{\mathrm{ext}} falls below one half beyond a finite time. In the model the retention limb is therefore a statement about the flat share of the property’s direction and about the map from budget to flow time, neither of which the model fixes; and the flat directions are where terms beyond the second order decide what happens, so the model is least reliable there.

Two installations.

The embedded installation is one candidate reading of “with correction embedded in the training objective”, which P23’s entry fixes operationally: the installing examples enter the objective under which capability is formed, from its first step and at a fixed share, up to the installation point (registration version 1.105, P23, its first fixed thing). In the model the property is raised while the original capability loss, with curvature Φ0\Phi_0 and eigenvalues λi0\lambda^0_i about ω0\omega_0, stays in the objective, a local reading of that definition and not the definition. Gradient flow for a joint time τj\tau_{\mathrm{j}} on that loss with a positive weight on VV moves the system by a displacement proportional to (I−e−Φ0τj)Φ0−1g(I - e^{-\Phi_0\tau_{\mathrm{j}}})\Phi_0^{-1} g (Appendix A.8); as τj\tau_{\mathrm{j}} grows, with Φ0\Phi_0 positive definite, it tends to the displacement that installs a given effect at least capability cost, wemb=Y(0)Φ0−1g/(g⊤Φ0−1g)w_{\mathrm{emb}} = Y(0)\,\Phi_0^{-1} g/(g^\top\Phi_0^{-1} g).

Proposition IV-L (the cost of the two installations; the report’s own models, not registered). Measured by the original loss at second order, the capability cost of installing an effect Y(0)Y(0) is 12Y(0)2(g⊤Φ0g)/|g|4\tfrac{1}{2}Y(0)^2\,(g^\top\Phi_0 g)/|g|^4 for the external installation and 12Y(0)2/(g⊤Φ0−1g)\tfrac{1}{2}Y(0)^2/(g^\top\Phi_0^{-1} g) for the embedded one, and the second is never the larger. (Proof: Appendix A.8.)

The cost is the second-order form Mirzadeh et al. (2020) use for forgetting, and the least-cost displacement under one linear constraint is the Lagrangian solution Hassibi and Stork (1992) give for a constraint on one weight (Section 2).

Assumption S (later training of the same kind). Φ\Phi and Φ0\Phi_0 share eigenvectors, and their eigenvalues are similarly ordered on the directions the property depends on: (λi0−λi′0)(λi−λi′)≥0(\lambda^0_i - \lambda^0_{i'})(\lambda_i - \lambda_{i'}) \ge 0 for every two such directions ii and i′i'. Where the original loss is stiffer along one of them than along another, the later loss is at least as stiff along the first. Φ=Φ0\Phi = \Phi_0 (more training on the same loss) is the purest case; Φ=cΦ0\Phi = c\,\Phi_0 with c>0c > 0, and Φ0\Phi_0 plus a common multiple of the identity (the same loss with weight decay), are others.

Theorem IV-C (the comparison, under Assumption S; the report’s own models, not registered). Under Assumption S, with Φ0\Phi_0 positive definite on the directions the property depends on and the two installed effects matched, Semb(τ)≥Sext(τ)S_{\mathrm{emb}}(\tau) \ge S_{\mathrm{ext}}(\tau) at every τ≥0\tau \ge 0, with equality at τ>0\tau > 0 exactly when λi0\lambda^0_i or λi\lambda_i is constant on those directions; and the ratio Semb(τ)/Sext(τ)S_{\mathrm{emb}}(\tau)/S_{\mathrm{ext}}(\tau) does not fall as τ\tau grows. (Proof: Appendix A.9.)

Corollary IV-C$'$ (joint training stopped at a finite time; the report’s own models, not registered). Under Assumption S, an installation by joint training stopped at any time τj>0\tau_{\mathrm{j}} > 0 also retains at least as large a fraction as the external one, at every τ\tau, with no condition on Φ0\Phi_0 beyond Assumption S; and its retained fraction does not fall as τj\tau_{\mathrm{j}} lengthens, tending to SextS_{\mathrm{ext}} as τj\tau_{\mathrm{j}} tends to zero and, where Φ0\Phi_0 is positive definite on the property’s directions, to SembS_{\mathrm{emb}} as τj\tau_{\mathrm{j}} grows. (Proof: Appendix A.10.)

In words: under Assumption S, later training of the same kind, a gain installed with the capability loss in the objective retains at least as large a fraction as one installed by external post-training, and the ratio of the two does not fall with training; where the later loss’s curvature is unrelated to the original’s, the embedded installation can retain less. An oppositely ordered later curvature reverses the inequality, and where the two eigenbases differ the embedded weights can take either sign, so that what was installed can turn into a deficit. So the model predicts a moderator: a change of capability domain that reorders curvature along the property’s directions can undo the embedded advantage, and a unit that does not report which case its later training was in cannot be read against it. Of the two installations, the one that costs less capability is, under Assumption S, also the one later training erodes less; the cost ordering holds always, the retention ordering only under Assumption S. A worked case: two directions with curvatures 44 and 1/41/4, Φ=Φ0\Phi = \Phi_0 and g=(1,1)g = (1, 1) in that basis; at τ=1\tau = 1 the external installation retains 0.399 and the embedded one 0.734, the external having cost 4.5 times as much capability; at τ=1/2\tau = 1/2 the external figure is 0.509, so which side of one half it falls on depends on the flow time the model leaves unfixed; and with the later curvatures in the opposite order, 1/41/4 and 44, the embedded installation retains 0.063 at τ=1\tau = 1. A weight decay towards a reference common to both runs adds the same constant to every eigenvalue of Φ\Phi, keeps Assumption S, and multiplies both retained fractions by one factor (Section 9).

The ordering is weak, and P23’s margin is not a theorem.

Theorem IV-C orders the two arms only weakly.
